newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil govt wins CVRD court victory.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil govt wins CVRD court victory.

text.p: The Brazilian government won a crucial legal victory on Monday when a high court judge revoked a host of injunctions blocking the privatization of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD).

A spokesman for Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said officials believed the judge's ruling overturned all the court orders that had been stopping Latin America's largest state sell-off to date from going ahead.
"We still have to see the order, but the understanding among our lawyers is that this is the case," he said.
The sale of 45 percent of CVRD's voting stock was due to have begun on April 29 but has been delayed repeatedly by court action.

The government appealed to the Superior Court of Justice in Brasilia, the country's highest court for non-constitutional matters, arguing that all law suits should be considered by a single tribunal because of a "conflict of interpretation".
An official at the court said Justice Democrito Reinaldo had agreed with the government's view and named a federal court in Rio de Janeiro as the tribunal responsible for all CVRD cases.

The phrasing of Reinaldo's statement, however, which said he had suspended "the injunctions which were among the 27 cases studied," did not immediately make clear whether it also applied to a new injunction issued in Rio Monday.
It remained unclear whether the auction would go ahead Monday evening though officials said they were doubtful.
Brazil hopes to raise at least $5 billion from the sale of the world's largest iron ore exporter, making it the biggest Latin American privatization to date.
But the sell-off of the jewel in the Brazilian public sector's crown has been controversial.
Demonstrators clashed with police in downtown Rio last week and a chorus of criticism has risen from past presidents, Catholic bishops and the judiciary.
Monday's O Globo newspaper said the delay was beginning to irritate the leader of one of the two consortia bidding.

"It's a very unpleasant situation," Globo quoted Antonio Ermirio de Moraes, chief executive of Brazil's largest private conglomerate Votorantim, as saying. Votorantim heads the Valecom consortium together with South Africa's Anglo American Corp.
Moraes said Brazil was putting on a "Third World show" and complained that the delay was costing his partners money.
According to Globo, the government also was losing out, having had to spend $280,000 on the documents for its high court case alone.
